events.title: How Your Immune System Learns
events.location: Hewlett Teaching Center, 370 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA 94305, 201
events.abstract:
Abstract: In humans’ immune response, B cells that produce high-affinity (strongly binding) antibodies are generated through a Darwinian evolutionary process called “affinity maturation”. Affinity maturation, which takes place in germinal centers (GCs), is driven by cycles of selection (mediated by T cells), division, and hypermutation of B cells. Recently, it was found that the T cells themselves also exhibit dynamic behavior throughout the course of the GC reaction, undergoing affinity-dependent proliferation. A model suggests that this reciprocal stimulation enforces a robust “homeostatic” regulation of the relative number of B cells and T cells in the GC, leading to a constant ratio of T cells to B cells. But the model also points to a problem: the high mutation rate of GC B cells can lead to “backsliding” of affinity. The proposed solution – a fitness-dependent mutation rate – has been experimentally verified, and has implications beyond B cell affinity maturation.
Ned Wingreen is the Howard A. Prior Professor of the Life Sciences at Princeton University. He is a member of the Department of Molecular Biology and Associate Director of the Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics, where he is Director of Graduate Studies of the QCB Graduate Program. He is also associated faculty in the Department of Physics. Ned received his Ph.D. in theoretical condensed matter physics from Cornell University in 1989. He did his postdoc in mesoscopic physics at MIT before moving, in 1991, to the NEC Research Institute in Princeton. At NEC, he continued to work in mesoscopic physics, but also started research in biophysics which grew into a general interest in problems at the interface of physics and biology. Ned joined Princeton University in 2004. Ned's current research focuses on modeling of bacteria, bacterial communities, phages, and other microorganisms, as well as studies of intracellular phase separation, and topics in immunology. Abstract: Most natural diamonds form at depths of 120 to 200 km in Earth’s lithospheric mantle. A small fraction, however, originates much deeper. This group of diamonds, known as sublithospheric diamonds, includes some of the largest and finest diamonds in the world. These diamonds can contain mineral inclusions that represent some of the deepest samples of Earth’s interior. In this talk, I will show how the chemistry of these inclusions records the geological history experienced by their host diamonds, providing a unique window into the dynamic processes that have shaped our planet over time.

His research focuses on understanding the large-scale geochemical processes that have shaped Earth, Moon, and other terrestrial bodies throughout their formation, differentiation, and evolution. His group combines a wide range of approaches, including non-traditional stable isotope geochemistry, high-pressure high-temperature experiments, studies of natural sample studies, and geochemical modeling. His recent work includes investigating the recycling of surface materials into Earth’s deep interior using diamond inclusions; studying Apollo samples to better understand the Moon’s volatile budget and volcanic activity; and experimentally constraining the behavior of moderately volatile elements during evaporation processes.

events.title: New frontier of Quantum Computing
events.location: Hewlett Teaching Center, 370 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA 94305, 201
events.abstract:
A broad effort is currently underway to develop quantum computers that can outperform classical counterparts for certain computational, simulation or sensing tasks. The practical realization of such systems and exploration of their potential capabilities and limitations are central themes in the new field of quantum science and engineering. A central challenge in quantum computing is error suppression, which requires quantum error correction for large-scale processing. However, the overhead involved in creating error-corrected "logical" qubits-where information is redundantly encoded across multiple physical qubits-presents a significant obstacle to scalable quantum computing. In this talk, we will discuss recent advances in the programmable, coherent manipulation of quantum systems using neutral atom arrays excited into Rydberg states. These advances allow control over several hundred qubits and the exploration of quantum algorithms with encoded logical qubits and quantum error correction techniques. Enabled by the remarkable interdisciplinary effort, involving academia and industry, these advances have redefined the frontier of quantum computing and quantum information. They herald the advent of early error-corrected quantum computation, paving the way for new applications and inspiring a shift in addressing both the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead. Several examples of emerging applications, ranging from quantum many-body physics to quantum computing enhanced imaging will be discussed.
Dr. Mikhail Lukin is the Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor of Physics at Harvard University, where he also serves as Co-Director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative. Dr. Lukin received his Ph.D. in physics from Texas A&M University. Dr. Lukin’s research focuses on quantum optics and quantum information science, with an emphasis on controlling strongly interacting atomic, optical, and solid-state systems. His work explores the quantum dynamics of many-body systems and develops novel applications in quantum computing, quantum simulation, quantum communication, and metrology. Dr. Lukin has pioneered advances in neutral atom quantum computing, quantum networking, and quantum sensing with both atomic and atom-like solid-state systems. Dr. Lukin has authored more than 540 scientific publications and is a member or fellow of the National Academy of Sciences, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Physical Society, and Optica. His honors include the Physics World Breakthrough of the Year (2024), Falling Walls Breakthrough of the Year in Physical Sciences (2023), the International Quantum Award (2022), the Norman F. Ramsey Prize of the American Physical Society (2022), the Charles Hard Townes Award of Optica (2021), the George Gamow Award (2020), and the Vannevar Bush Faculty Fellowship (2015). Earlier in his career, Dr. Lukin was recognized with the Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship, the Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering, and the NSF CAREER Award. Today, Dr. Lukin continues to advance quantum information science through both research and leadership, helping shape the future of computing, communication, and measurement at the frontiers of physics.

events.title: ESE Seminar - Ruben Juanes: "Photoporomechanics: Towards stress-tensor tomography in 3D granular media"
events.abstract:
Abstract
Ruben Juanes (joint work with Wei Li, Yue Meng, Shiyao Wang)
Photoporomechanics: Towards stress-tensor tomography in 3D granular mediaRuben Juanes (joint work with Wei Li, Yue Meng, Shiyao Wang)At a fundamental level, the macroscopic response of granular media depends on the spatial organization of contact forces between grains—the so-called force chains. Despite their critical importance, force chains in granular media have been characterized and analyzed almost exclusively in 2D systems. To address this knowledge gap, we recently developed a new approach: a tomographic imaging technique (interference optical projection tomography, or IOPT), which by combining the principles of photoelasticity and tomography, provides direct visualization of the particles’ force network, thus circumventing the need of constitutive models of particle-particle contact (Li and Juanes, 2024). With our novel experimental technique, we provide the microscopic explanation for why a pack of angular particles is stronger than one of round particles: they form interconnected force networks that are less likely to buckle when under stress than the isolated chains in a pack of round particles.While early results show the potential of our approach, currently this new technique is limited to reconstructing the 3D scalar field of stress-anisotropy under axisymmetric stressconditions, for example, triaxial shear. Here, we present the reconstruction of the grain-scale full tensor field in 3D (stress-tensor tomography) and focus on the study of the 3D internal stresses in a single particle subject to arbitrary loading conditions. If time permits, we will present early results extending the experimentation, modeling, and inversion of the stress field from the single-particle scale to the ensemble-scale of 3D granular packs. The ability to interrogate the grain-scale stresses in granular media will enable new understanding of granular media and help predict the behavior of fluid-coupled granular media in landslides, liquefaction, and earthquakes.
Bio
Ruben Juanes is professor in Civil and Environmental Engineering, and Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences at MIT, where he has been since 2006. He is an expert in fluid flow through porous media and in geomechanics, and has applied his research to the fields of energy resources, carbon capture and storage, gas hydrates, water infiltration and soil irrigation, and induced seismicity. He holds an undergraduate degree from University of A Coruña (Spain) and graduate degrees from UC Berkeley, all in Civil and Environmental Engineering. He is a fellow of the American Geophysical Union and the American Physical Society.

events.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Gregor Steinbrügge- "Coupled Thermal-Orbital Evolution of the Galilean Satellites"
events.abstract:
Io's volcanism and Europa's surface bear witness to the dynamics driven by tidal interactions of the Galilean moons with Jupiter. While Europa and Ganymede host subsurface oceans, which makes them prime candidates for habitability, tidal heating is unlikely to have been constant over the age of the Laplace resonance. In this talk I will revisit the coupled thermal–orbital evolution of the Galilean satellites using the astrometric and geophysical constraints obtained over the past years. The Juno mission has provided additional data about geodetic parameters and recent ground-based observations indicate that Io has been volcanically active for most of its history, with potentially higher activity at earlier times. We also apply lessons learned from the Saturn system, particularly informed by the Cassini mission, to investigate the possibility of ‘resonance locking’ as the dominant mechanism driving the orbital migration of Io. Our analysis shows that considering ‘resonance locking’ in the Jovian system could reveal new evolutionary paths with early tidal dissipation in Ganymede and periodic inward migration of Io. I will further discuss the implications for the structure and dynamics of Europa’s ice shell if ‘resonance’ locking is at play. Finally, I will outline how some of these hypotheses can be tested by the Europa Clipper mission.
Gregor Steinbrügge received his M.S. degree in physics from the Free University of Berlin, Germany, in 2013 and completed his Ph.D. at the Institute of Geodesy and Geoinformation Science of the Technical University of Berlin, Germany, in 2018. His thesis on tidal interactions across the Solar System was completed in collaboration with the Institute of Planetary Research at the German Aerospace Center (DLR). He is a Research Scientist at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the Investigation Scientist for REASON (Radar for Europa Assessment and Sounding: Ocean to Near-surface). He is also a Co-Investigator on the BepiColombo Laser Altimeter (BELA) and on the Ganymede Laser Altimeter (GALA) aboard Juice, and a member of the VenSAR science team on ESA's EnVision mission. His research focuses on tidal interactions of planetary bodies in our Solar System, ice geophysics, radar and laser geodesy, and the development of innovative mission instrumentation.

Talk Title: Heart-brain interactions driving cardiovascular dysfunction
Speaker: Alexander R. Nectow, MD, PhD Assistant Professor, Department of Medicine, Columbia University

LOCATION: Lokey Stem Cell Research Building , G1161 Large Conference Room

ABOUT THE TALK
Stress is a major trigger of arrhythmia, yet the mechanisms underlying these effects remain poorly defined. Using a genetic model of ventricular tachycardia (VT), we find that naturalistic emotional stressors rapidly provoke malignant arrhythmias in vulnerable hearts. By tracing back from sympathetic neurons innervating myocardium, we identify a multi-synaptic, brain-to-heart circuit originating within the midbrain, which is required for stress-induced VT. Strikingly, activation of this pathway induces VT within seconds, suggesting that central neuronal control of the heart is an important arrhythmogenic trigger. Together, this work identifies a brain-to-heart circuit responsible for triggering stress-induced arrhythmias and points toward circuit-directed therapies for this class of tachyarrhythmias.
ABOUT THE SPEAKER
Alexander Nectow, MD, PhD, is an Assistant Professor at Columbia University who has established the dorsal raphe nucleus as a new center in the brain's control of feeding and energy homeostasis. The group has identified defined dorsal raphe and adjacent brainstem cell populations whose activity drives food intake and energy expenditure using cell type-specific molecular profiling and circuit dissection tools, many developed in the lab. Together, this work has established new principles for the neural control of feeding at the cell type and circuit level. The lab now runs two active programs: continued mechanistic work on the neural control of energy balance, and a newer effort on the brain-heart axis – the central afferent and efferent circuits that govern cardiac physiology, and their contributions to arrhythmia and other cardiovascular disease

events.title: PhD Dissertation Defense: Tianyu Lu
events.abstract:
Title: Generative Models for Protein Design
Abstract: Generative models are flexible tools with which we can model complex data distributions. When applied to proteins, we aim to build a model capable of generalizing the patterns observed in natural protein sequence/structure/function to the design of novel proteins conditioned on arbitrary desired functions. Samples from a generative model are hypotheses of the physical world. I show that generative models can expand functional space beyond what nature has already explored. First, I propose the SHAPES framework to benchmark how well generative models cover the distribution of native protein structures. I present the perspective of an oracle trap, in which filtering designs by structure prediction models leads to oversampling of idealized helices and undersampling of loops. Second, I present Protpardelle-1c, a collection of generative models of protein structure with improved conditional generation capabilities. I focus on motif scaffolding, in which we can condition on function by identifying a substructure/subsequence pair which geometrically defines the desired function. Protpardelle-1c excels on MotifBench, a standardized benchmark for motif scaffolding, proposing designable scaffolds to problems previously unsolved by other models. Finally, I apply generative models to the design of lanthanide binding proteins. I demonstrate how partial diffusion with Protpardelle-1c allows access to local perturbations of the lanmodulin fold to unearth a previously unexplored sequence space which has inverted rare earth selectivity, favoring heavy rare earths over light rare earths. Given a feedstock initially enriched in La/Ce (70%), the designed protein removes ~99% of lanthanum and cerium to enrich for more valuable heavy rare earths. I also validate motif scaffolding experimentally, showing that EF hands hosted in novel non-lanmodulin scaffolds recapitulate their intended selectivity profiles, and use this to probe the modularity of selectivity and the interplay between motif and scaffold.

events.title: Earth & Planetary Sciences Seminar - Prof. Esteban Gazel "Bioleaching of critical elements from ultramafic minerals with synthetic biology"
events.abstract:
Abstract: As the world demand for critical elements needed for energy storage (e.g., Ni, Co, Cr) exponentially increases, the need for non-conventional sources becomes more urgent. Ultramafic minerals are an important reservoir of these energy-critical elements, but they are bound within silicate structures making it challenging to separate them, and thus most current mined sources are laterites. These deposits resulted from extensive weathering, taking geologic time scales for dissolution and concentration. Carbon mineralization of ultramafic rocks is also a promising approach for long-term carbon dioxide removal from the atmosphere. Therefore, a strategy for accelerating weathering of ultramafic rocks is fundamental. We investigated whether an engineered strain of Gluconobacter oxydans (engineered strain, B58 ∆pstS, P112:mgdh) can accelerate weathering to simultaneously bioleach critical elements (e.g., Ni) and sequester carbon from ultramafic minerals (olivine and enstatitie). These minerals were bioleached at low-temperature conditions (30 C) and with up to 60% pulp density in direct contact with the engineered microbes and by separating the biolixiviant from the living cells. Experiments with direct interaction of G. oxydans with ultramafic minerals evolved from white to dark red/brown, witch likely resulted from a redox reaction (Fe2+ to Fe3+). This reaction has been observed where microbes oxidize Fe as an energy source or to limit Fe2+ toxicity. We also found that G. oxydans interaction with ultramafic minerals also enables the precipitation of magnesium oxalate, a pathway with twice the carbon storage capacity of magnesite. Oxalic acid was identified in the biolixiviant produced by G. oxydans and Mg-oxalate formation was most efficient at low pH. SEM and XRD analyses indicate extensive olivine dissolution and coating by Mg-oxalate and amorphous silica. Mass balance calculations suggest that G. oxydans leached up to 75% of the Mg hosted in the starting materials, while only 11% of leached Mg reacted to sequester carbon as Mg-oxalate after 15 days. During this time the solution reached ~8000 pm Mg and ~80 ppm Ni, leaving only 25% of Mg in the residual olivine that did not react. The enhanced sequestration potential of Mg-oxalate, coupled with bio-accelerated critical element leaching presents a promising opportunity for global carbon storage and opens a new, non-conventional, sources of critical elements.
Speaker Bio: Esteban Gazel is the Charles N. Mellowes Professor in Engineering at the Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at Connell University. He got his PhD in 2009 from Rutgers University, followed by a postdoctoral fellowship at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. From 2011-2017, he was an assistant and associate professor at Virginia Tech, and in 2017, moved to Cornell. He got the early career Kuno Award of AGU in 2016 and just became a Mineralogical Society of America Fellow. His lab investigates magma reservoirs, melt transport, degassing, and their role in the formation of ore deposits. He is also working on understanding element fractionation, transport, and accumulation to discover and utilize non-conventional critical mineral deposits and develop new critical elemental extraction processes (i.e., biomining)

events.title: ESE Seminar - Boryann Liaw: "Building Sustainable Artificial Intelligence-Guided Energy Systems from Fundamental Science"
events.abstract:
Abstract
Future society needs a sustainable energy supply to support economic growth, and artificial intelligence (AI)-aided, data-driven approaches are rapidly transforming the energy landscape. Sustaining this momentum requires solutions that are both cost effective and energy efficient. The current approach relies on heuristic methods and intensive data acquisition, but resource constraints make rapid deployment difficult. Quantifying returns on investment while accounting for uncertainty and risk adds another major challenge. A trustworthy framework is therefore essential to guide this transformation—but how can such a framework be built?
Physics-informed framework has been often proposed as a safeguard for the data-driven paradigm. To make this paradigm trustworthy, however, its physics-informed foundation must be reinforced through fundamental science. This presentation will discuss how empirical reduction and induction can strengthen that foundation through quantification and verification. The goal is to ensure that regression-model predictions not only obey fundamental principles but are also quantitatively interpretable. This would connect controlled laboratory test data with real-world, live data streams for practical applications. Because limited data transferability has become a major bottleneck, a quantitative and verifiable physics-informed framework could help overcome it and accelerate a sustainable transformation that is both cost-effective and energy-efficient.
Bio
Dr. Boryann (Bor Yann) Liaw is a Guest Professor at Forschungszentrum Jülich in Germany. He brings four decades of experience in research and development involving electrochemical energy conversion and storage. He earned his Ph.D. in Materials Science and Engineering from Stanford University in 1988. From 2016 to 2023, he served as a Directorate Fellow and Department Manager at Idaho National Laboratory. Previously, from 1989 to 2016, he was a tenured faculty member at the University of Hawaii at Manoa. He has also been a visiting scientist at Sandia National Laboratories and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Since founding HPRL in 1996, he has served as a consultant to private companies and an advisor to research institutions.
Dr. Liaw’s research focuses on rechargeable batteries, fuel cells, energy-storage technologies, charging infrastructure for electrification, energy harvesting, and data-informed technologies. His work includes laboratory and large-scale field evaluations of batteries and electric vehicles, as well as performance analysis, diagnosis, and prognosis. He has also developed in-depth expertise in battery modeling and simulation, performance and life prediction, fast charging, and the analysis of battery aging, degradation, and failure. His broader energy-conversion and storage research encompasses biofuel cells, sugar-air alkaline batteries, and methods for converting harvested energy resources into useful power sources for mobile and stationary applications.

His recent honors include the 2022 Research Award from The Electrochemical Society’s Battery Division, the 2020 Technology Award from the International Battery Association (IBA), and recognition as one of the 2019 Asian American Engineers of the Year by the National Society of Professional Engineers. He has co-authored more than 200 technical publications, including 10 book chapters, and has contributed to five edited books and 20 patents or patent applications.

Please join German Studies Lecture Series for Worlds in AI and the Novel, a conversation with Hannes Bajohr (UC Berkeley).
“A world—nothing less—is the theme and postulate of the novel,” Hans Blumenberg wrote in 1963, as AI research was beginning to develop its own “world models.” Today, these literary and computational senses of world converge in LLMs, whose latent spaces can generate narratives with striking coherence but often weak causality. Drawing on literary traditions from realism to modernism and on his own experiments with a fine-tuned German-language model, Professor Bajohr asks how novels and LLMs construct worlds through networks of relations, inferences, and expectations. The talk uses this comparison to situate AI-generated fiction between claims of machine understanding and dismissals of mere mimicry.

events.title: Geophysics Master's Presentation, Hamad Alswaidan: "Machine Learning-Assisted Full Waveform Inversion: Low-Frequency Extrapolation and Cycle-Skipping Mitigation"
events.abstract:
Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful technique for estimating subsurface physical properties from seismic data. However, its nonlinear nature and the limited availability of low-frequency seismic data make it susceptible to cycle skipping, often preventing convergence toward an accurate subsurface model.
In this work, Hamad explores two complementary machine learning approaches to address these challenges. The first investigates the use of generative diffusion models to extrapolate missing low-frequency content in seismic data. The second introduces a neural network-based approach to mitigate cycle skipping through the alignment of observed and modeled seismic waveforms during inversion.
Together, these approaches explore how machine learning can complement physics-based inversion and improve the robustness of FWI.

If representation is an act of conferring visibility, this power is now challenged by visual generative AI and highly realistic synthetic images of war and conflict. So far, research on visual generative AI in the context of war and conflict representation has mostly focused on the representational implications of AI-generated images and their role in adding fuel to information disorder. In this talk, I shift attention to the technological infrastructures of image generators and stock image sites that incentivize and at times blatantly encourage curation of such images. By unpacking the relationship between the production, representation and circulation of AI-generated images of the Russia-Ukraine war, I discuss methodological challenges and potential solutions to studying AI-mediated commercialization and visual construction of war.

events.title: Ergodic Theory, categorically
events.abstract: In recent years, categorical treatments of famous theorems about properties of invariant measures have emerged. Among them are the de Finetti Theorem, the strong law of large numbers and ergodic decompositions. Here, we synthesize these developments by introducing the concept of a mixing morphism for an abstract dynamical system in a Markov category. It axiomatizes the idea of finding an average of the dynamics that is itself invariant, which is closely tied to the Pointwise Ergodic Theorem. In this talk, we will explore the abstract consequences of having a mixing morphism as well as several concrete instantiations in familiar Markov categories - for general probabilistic systems, linear systems with Gaussian noise, and possibilistic uncertainty.

Konstantina Stankovic, MD, PhD: Bertarelli Foundation Professor and Chair, Stanford University
Bio: Konstantina “Tina” Stankovic, MD, PhD, FACS is the Bertarelli Foundation Professor and Chair of the Department of Otolaryngology – Head & Neck Surgery at Stanford University School of Medicine, and professor, by courtesy, of Neurosurgery. She is a Harvard-trained ear and skull-base surgeon and a Massachusetts Institute of Technology-trained auditory neuroscientist. She blends her surgical expertise with training in physics, molecular biology, auditory neuroscience, and systems electrophysiology to devise novel solutions tailored to the unmet needs of those with hearing loss. She has initiated and led cross-departmental, national, and international collaborations to develop and deploy novel molecular diagnostics and therapeutics for hearing loss and otologic diseases in general while educating the next generation of leaders in surgery and science. Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been used in many areas of medicine, and large language models (LLMs) have shown potential utility for various clinical applications. However, to determine if LLMs can accelerate the pace of genetic diagnosis and discovery, we examined whether recently developed LLMs (Med-PaLM 2 and Gemini) could assist in solving four types of genetic problems, which had sequentially increased complexity. First, in response to free-text input, Med-PaLM 2 correctly identified murine genes with experimentally verified causative genetic factors for six previously studied murine models for biomedical traits. Second, Med-PaLM 2 identified a novel causative murine genetic factor for spontaneous hearing loss that was validated using knock-in mice. Third, we developed a retrieval and grounding pipeline that enabled Gemini 2.5 Pro to analyze large lists of genes with genetic variants, which were identified in the genomic sequences of 20 human subjects with hearing loss; and it identified causative genetic factors for 80% of these subjects. Fourth, we developed a genetic analysis pipeline, which enabled the modified Gemini 2.5 Pro without any task-specific fine-tuning to identify causative genetic factors for six subjects with rare genetic diseases that required 14 to 34 different terms to describe their multi-faceted symptom complex. These results demonstrate that an AI pipeline can facilitate genetic diagnosis and discovery in mice and humans.

Amy E. Herr
Chancellor’s Professor, Department of Bioengineering
University of California, Berkeley
Title: What Genes (and Transcripts) Can't Tell You: Single-Cell Proteomic Tools for Embryos to Ecosystems
Abstract: Proteins are the primary functional molecules of the cell. A protein’s molecular form, abundance, and subcellular localization control cellular decision-making in ways that DNA and RNA cannot predict. Even at single-cell resolution, sequencing tools are blind to proteoforms, post-translational modifications, and protein-level heterogeneity that distinguish one cell's functional state from another's. Inspired by how microfluidic innovations — from droplet encapsulation and flow cells to nanopore integration — enabled the single-cell sequencing revolution, my lab designs precision proteomic tools capable of capturing both cellular- and protein-level heterogeneity.
We pursue this vision across applications spanning clinical biomedicine to fundamental biology. In breast cancer, we partner with physician-scientists to assess whether patient-derived tumor organoids faithfully recapitulate the therapeutic responses of the patients from whom they were derived — deploying single-cell mass spectrometry proteomics to profile protein states across organoid cell populations with single-cell resolution. In developmental biology, we measure the proteomic basis of lineage commitment in individual blastomeres of pre-implantation mouse embryos, using same-cell assays that recover both protein and RNA from the same originating cell — eliminating the between-cell noise that confounds separate-cell multi-omic comparisons. We extend this ‘joint analyses’ approach to organoid-derived cells, by coupling proteome and open chromatin (snATAC-seq). At a global scale, we collaborate with marine biologists to identify the molecular drivers of coral bleaching, the breakdown of symbiosis between coral host cells and their algal partners that threatens reef ecosystems worldwide.
What unifies our questions is a shared analytical challenge: rare, precious, or highly heterogeneous cell populations where bulk averaging is not just imprecise but misleading. In many cases, there is a need for sub-cellular measurement insight. Across all of the applications, I will detail how microfluidic design seamlessly integrates unit functions, precisely controls transport and reaction, and scales up efficiently. I will also consider the opportunities these tools create as AI/ML models of cellular behavior (i.e., virtual cell initiatives) increasingly demand paired, ground-truth molecular measurements at single-cell resolution.
Bio: Amy E. Herr received a BS degree in Engineering & Applied Science from the California Institute of Technology and MS and PhD degrees in Mechanical Engineering from Stanford University, where she was an NSF Graduate Research Fellow. She holds a Chancellor’s Professorship at the University of California, Berkeley in the Department of Bioengineering and is a Chan Zuckerberg Biohub Investigator. Prior to joining UC Berkeley, she was a staff member in the Biosystems Research Group at Sandia National Laboratories (Livermore, CA). Her research interests include bioinstrumentation innovation to advance quantitation in the biosciences & biomedicine, in particular the study and application of electrokinetic phenomena in single-cell and sub-cellular analyses. Her pedagogical interests are in bioengineering design and transport. Professor Herr is an elected Fellow of the American Institute of Medical and Biological Engineering (AIMBE) and an elected member of the National Academy of Inventors (2017). She serves on the DARPA Biological Science and Technology (BSAT) working group and the Engineering Review Committee for Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. She is an Associate Editor at the Royal Society of Chemistry’s journal Lab on a Chip.

"Predicting Spectroscopic Responses and Reactivity in Condensed-Phase Environments: Mechanistic Insights into Photophysics and Catalysis"
Local molecular environments influence the structural dynamics and electronic properties of the systems and determine how molecules respond to light and undergo chemical reactions. Predicting these responses requires linking environmental effects to experimental observables and molecular functions. In this talk, I will present computational frameworks that connect environmental interactions with spectroscopic responses, photodynamic pathways, and catalytic behavior.
I will first introduce an ab initio approach to quantify the vibrational Stark effect and environment-induced frequency shifts. While experimental spectra provide an ensemble-averaged picture, simulations reveal how individual molecular conformations and their local electric fields contribute to their frequency shifts. I will then discuss the extension of this framework to liver alcohol dehydrogenase (LADH2), examining how the protein environment affects the vibrational frequencies of bonds involved in the reaction. These responses offer insights into the physical origins of catalytic rate enhancement and future mutation studies.
Next, I will present excited state dynamics studies of red fluorescent proteins. Excited-state simulations reveal how residue protonation states and hydrogen-bonding interactions regulate chromophore twisting and non-radiative decay. These mechanisms help predict differences in fluorescence brightness and suggest molecular features to target in future protein designs.
Together, these studies connect spectroscopic features to molecular-level mechanisms, providing a physical foundation for understanding and tuning molecular behavior in condensed-phase environments.

"Automatically discovering multistep mechanisms for rapid reaction network construction"
Rapid and accurate construction of reaction networks (RN) is of paramount importance in chemistry. The rate limiting step in RN construction is finding relevant transition states (TS) on the potential energy surface. Algorithms like the Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) are standard workhorses when a reactant and product pair are known. However, these methods assume the input geometries are one TS away. This assumption is routinely broken when the input minima come from enhanced sampling dynamics or "template"-based approaches, where a multi-step mechanism is required to carry out the transformation, such as through rearrangements into reactive conformers. We present an adaptive algorithm that automatically identifies reaction intermediates and splits into separate path minimizations. Splitting enables competing pathway exploration, turning the TS search problem into a mini-network construction one. We showcase its potential and limitations using known multi-step reactions, successfully reproducing the mechanisms autonomously.

Physical Chemistry Seminar: Professor Connor Coley, MIT
events.abstract:
About the Seminar
"AI and the Expanding Computational Toolbox for Chemistry"
Chemistry has a long history of incorporating computation to understand molecules, predict behavior, and guide discovery. Progress in artificial intelligence, cheminformatics, and optimization methods has accelerated this trajectory, expanding the scale and scope of problems that can be approached computationally. Although many core challenges in chemistry remain far from solved, the computational tools available to chemists have advanced rapidly in both capability and accessibility, creating new opportunities to explore chemical space and reason about molecular systems. In this lecture, I will discuss our recent progress developing new computational methods for structure elucidation, synthetic organic chemistry, and small molecule design.
About the Speaker
Connor W. Coley is the Warren K. Lewis Associate Professor in Chemical Engineering and an Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at MIT in the Schwarzman College of Computing. His research group works at the interface of AI and chemistry to develop models that understand how molecules behave, interact, and react and use that knowledge to engineer new ones, with an emphasis on therapeutic discovery. He received his B.S. in Chemical Engineering from Caltech and his Ph.D. from MIT, followed by postdoctoral training at the Broad Institute.
Connor’s work has been recognized with the NSF CAREER Award (2021), C&EN’s “Talented Twelve” (2018), Forbes 30 Under 30: Healthcare (2019), Technology Review’s 35 Innovators Under 35 (2023), and the Bayer Early Excellence in Science Award (2021), among other honors. He was named as a Schmidt AI2050 Early Career Fellow (2022), Samsung AI Researcher of the Year (2023), Scialog Fellow (2024), and Camille Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar (2025), and was selected for the NAE Frontiers of Engineering Symposium (2025) and the Kavli Foundation Emerging Leader in Chemistry Lecture (2026). Connor has been further recognized for his teaching and mentorship by MIT’s inaugural Common Ground Award for Excellence in Teaching (2023), the Outstanding UROP Mentor Award (2024), and the James W. Swan Outstanding Faculty Award for Graduate Teaching in Chemical Engineering (2024, 2025, 2026).
Outside of MIT, Connor is a scientific advisor to several companies pursuing AI-driven discovery. He serves on the advisory boards of ACS Central Science, Chemical Science, and Digital Discovery, and is an Associate Editor of the Journal of the American Chemical Society.

events.title: Thesis Defense: Nicolas Robalin, N. Martinez Lab
events.abstract:
"Competition between two ancestral RNA modifying enzymes sets tRNA T-loop modification chemistries and tunes translation in human cells"
Transfer RNAs that decode mRNA during protein synthesis are the most densely modified RNAs in the cell. Uridine at position 54 is among the most evolutionarily conserved modified positions of the tRNA T-loop. Bacteria methylate this position to m5U54 while archaea pseudouridylate it to Ψ54. Humans inherited and kept enzymes from both ancestral lineages. However, the consequences of this dual inheritance and the functions of these modifications are unexplored. To address this, we depleted TRMT2A, the enzyme that installs m5U54, and profiled tRNAs using Nanopore and quantitative pseudouridine-sensitive tRNA sequencing, and mass spectrometry. We discovered that TRMT2A and the pseudouridine synthase PUS10 compete to modify the same uridine and set tRNA-specific m5U54 and Ψ54 occupancies. The competition shapes the proteome in a codon-specific manner, codons decoded by m5U54-modified tRNAs are translated more efficiently than those decoded by Ψ54-modified tRNAs. Further, we find a T-loop modification circuit that is inverted relative to the one defined in yeast. Together, our findings establish competition for distinct modifications at a single position as an epitranscriptomic mechanism of gene regulation and reveal that RNA modifications and their crosstalk circuits are neither universal nor static across domains of life.

events.title: Thesis Defense: Shuri Francis, Gaffney Group
events.abstract:
"Resolving the Charge Distributions and Lifetimes of Excited States in [Metal(diimine)(dithiolate)] Complexes with Ultrafast X-ray and Optical Absorption Spectroscopies"
"This thesis unravels the interplay between covalent metal–ligand interactions and the excited state charge distributions and lifetimes of planar d8 [M(diimine)(dithiolate)] complexes (M = Pt, Ni) with bipyridyl (bpy) and benzene-1,2-dithiolate (bdt) ligands, going beyond what was previously possible with nanosecond resolution optical transient absorption and photoemission spectroscopies. Due to the disproportionately strong metal–dithiolate orbital mixing that characterizes [M(R2-bpy)(bdt)] systems, the tunable, visible light HOMO → LUMO absorption bands of these chromophores have metal-and-dithiolate ligand → diimine ligand charge transfer (MLL’CT) character. The Pt (5d) congeners have been studied for decades and developed primarily as photosensitizers because of their long-lived 3MLL’CT states. Substituting the metal center renders these complexes non-luminescent, convoluting efforts to design more earth-abundant and cost-effective Ni (3d) alternatives. Towards rationally designing structurally asymmetric, photo-active systems that utilize charge transfer and/or metal-centered (d-d) excited states for photochemistry, it is necessary to understand how manipulating molecular design parameters controls excited state dynamics and structure immediately after light absorption.
Combining theoretical electronic structure studies with femtosecond resolution X-ray (XTA) and optical (OTA) transient absorption spectroscopies bridges this gap by elucidating fundamental design strategies to optimize excited state charge distributions and lifetimes in photo-active, mixed-ligand donor–acceptor transition metal complexes. Pt 2p3/2 (L3-edge) and Ni 1s (K-edge) XTA spectroscopies directly probe the metal center-specific excited state relaxation mechanisms of [M(bpy)(bdt)] complexes, implicating the low-lying unoccupied Ni 3dyz orbital of [Ni(bpy)(bdt)] in deactivating the MLL’CT state that is long-lived in [Pt(bpy)(bdt)]. This deactivation fosters, as the dominant decay channel, the sub-picosecond formation of a meta-stable triplet ligand field (3LF, ‘d-d’ symmetry) excited state that distorts along a tetrahedral structural coordinate. Moving from inner-sphere to outer-sphere modifications, OTA spectroscopy demonstrates that diimine ligand functionalization and solvation effects can be used to systematically adjust the excited state lifetime of [Ni(R2-bpy)(bdt)] systems. By integrating time-independent and time-dependent density functional theory (DFT/TDDFT) with the aforementioned ultrafast transient absorption experiments, pseudo-tetrahedral structural reorganization in the 3LF state is revealed to induce dynamic changes in metal–ligand orbital mixing, thereby reversing the directionality of the ligand-to-ligand charge transfer. In contrast, the long-lived 3MLL’CT state of [Pt(bpy)(bdt)] undergoes planar structural relaxation and maintains strong metal–dithiolate covalency. Unlike traditional metal-centered excited states, DFT calculations also show that diimine substituent groups and solvent polarity can be used to independently strengthen or weaken the partial metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) character that strong metal–ligand covalency grants the pseudo-tetrahedral 3LF state of [Ni(R2-bpy)(bdt)] complexes."

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar: Professor AJ Boydston, University of Wisconsin–Madison
events.abstract:
About the Seminar
"Photocatalysis to Enable Metal-Free ROMP and Multimaterial 3DP of Electronic Devices"
Our group integrates fundamental and applied research within the scope of soft materials. In this seminar, we will discuss a new mechanism for ring-opening metathesis polymerization that is now a centerpiece of our program. The approach leverages visible light photoredox catalysis to allow for the use of organic initiators, in contrast to widely used metal-alkylidene initiators. Studies on our mechanistic hypothesis have yielded an exciting interplay of challenges and opportunities, often with one disguised as the other. We will share our findings that include methods for stereocontrol, chain transfer, and increasing functional group compatibility, as well as our adventures into the applied and commercial sectors. Additionally, we will present a breakthrough application of photocatalysis in the field of 3D printing. Our bottom-up approach to multimaterial 3D printing leverages wavelength selectivity and chemical orthogonality to enable direct 3D printing of functioning electronic circuits. The technology build from our platform of Multimaterial Actinic Spatial Control (MASC) 3D printing and allows for simultaneous synthesis of insulating dielectric materials and metallic conductors from single, homogeneous resin formulations.
About the Speaker
Dr. Boydston began studying chemistry as an undergraduate at the University of Oregon under the guidance of Professor Michael M. Haley. His research focused on the synthesis and study of dehydrobenzoannulenes. After completing BS and MS degrees, he began doctoral research at the University of Texas at Austin. In 2005, Dr. Boydston joined the group of Professor Christopher W. Bielawski and was co-advised by Professor C. Grant Willson. Dr. Boydston completed his thesis research focused on the synthesis and applications of annulated bis(imidazolium) chromophores in 2007. After graduating, he moved to Pasadena, California to take an NIH postdoctoral position at the California Institute of Technology. There, he worked under the mentorship of Professor Robert H. Grubbs to develop new catalysts and methods for the synthesis and characterization of functionalized cyclic polymers. He returned to the Pacific Northwest as an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of Washington in the summer of 2010 and was promoted to Associate Professor with tenure in 2016. In August 2018, he moved to the Department of Chemistry at the University of Wisconsin as an Associate Professor of Chemistry and Yamamoto Family Professor of Chemistry. His research group currently focuses on developments in the areas of electro-organic synthesis, photoredox catalysis, polymer synthesis, mechanochemical transduction, triggered depolymerizations, polymers for therapeutic applications, and additive manufacturing (3D printing). His research and teaching efforts have been recognized through the NSF CAREER Award, Army Research Office Young Investigator Award, Cottrell Scholar Award, Camille Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar Award, and University of Washington Distinguished Teaching Award.

events.title: Thesis Defense: Frank Hu, Markland Group
events.abstract:
"Development of language modeling for chemical analysis and design"
Generative modeling techniques offer the opportunity to achieve intelligent and efficient molecular analysis and design, making their development critically important in areas ranging from small-molecule lead optimization to materials discovery. Language modeling techniques in particular have proven effective at navigating highly combinatorial, discrete design spaces, suggesting that similar approaches could transform molecular design. In this dissertation, I develop language-model-based methods for molecular applications. Beginning with the problem of property-directed generative design, I present an energy-based alignment algorithm for chemical language models that yields highly scalable and sample-efficient molecular generators. Next, I apply chemical language models to spectroscopic analysis by designing, implementing, scaling, and post-training an end-to-end deep learning model for small-molecule structure elucidation from one-dimensional NMR spectra, achieving accurate and efficient elucidation for systems with as many as 40 non-hydrogen atoms. I then extend this framework with retrosynthetic context to enable context-aware structure elucidation, substantially improving accuracy without degrading performance when only spectra are available. Finally, I demonstrate how multifidelity asynchronous reinforcement learning with large language models (LLMs) can achieve frontier-level performance in small-molecule lead optimization against an expensive in silico oracle. Together, these projects explore how neural sequence models can inform both the understanding and the practice of chemistry.

events.title: Thesis Defense: Braxton Bell, Huang Group
events.abstract:
"Computational design of chemically modified cyclic peptide binders"
Cyclic peptides are an exciting therapeutic modality as they bridge the gap between small molecule drugs and biologics like antibodies. Currently, the primary strategy for identifying cyclic peptide binders is through high throughput experimental screening of combinatorial libraries, offering little control over physicochemical properties or binding epitope. Recent deep learning-based computational tools can design cyclic peptide binders, but they are largely limited to modeling amide- and disulfide-closed macrocycles. We developed a structure-based computational method that can be used to design cyclic peptide binders with arbitrary chemical modifications and cyclization chemistries. For designing novel interfaces, we first employed a tertiary motif search approach by mining the Protein Data Bank for proteins containing structural elements resembling the target’s epitope surface. We extracted shape-complementary fragments interacting with this surface and then designed molecules exploiting these binding modes using a mixture of molecular dynamics and generative modeling to realize the peptide backbones. In benchmarks, our approach was competitive with existing deep learning-based approaches for interface design by in silico metrics while still supporting exotic chemistries. Experimentally, we designed and characterized TBMB-crosslinked bicycles and thioether-closed macrocycles against three target proteins: MDM2, B7-H3, and TROP2. Coupling design with high-throughput screening of focused libraries using cDNA display, we identified and matured our lead peptides to low nanomolar affinity. This work provides a framework for the development of the next generation of cyclic peptide design methods.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar: Professor Brooks Abel, University of California, Berkeley
events.abstract:
About the Seminar
"Organocatalysts for Controlled Cationic Ring-Opening Polymerizations"
Extensive efforts have been made to synthesize polymers derived from heterocyclic monomers including lactones, lactams, and epoxides among other monomers, and numerous synthetic routes have been developed for their controlled syntheses using anionic ring-opening polymerization (AROP) and coordination catalyst systems. Less explored but equally promising as sustainable materials are polymers derived from heterocyclic monomers that are best polymerized by cationic ring-opening polymerization (CROP). Polymers synthesized by CROP comprise a diverse range of functional groups including acetals, orthoesters, ethers, phosphates, and disulfides among others. Additionally, polymers synthesized by CROP have been explored for their biodegradability and chemical recycling to monomer. However, despite more than half a century of development, CROP of heterocyclic monomers has not yet reached the same level of control over molecular weight, microstructure, architecture, and stereochemistry as has been achieved for AROP systems. This is largely due to undesirable Lewis acid-base interactions between the CROP catalyst and heterocyclic monomer. This presentation will provide an overview of our recent efforts toward the development of organocatalysts for cationic ring-opening polymerizations.
About the Speaker
Brooks Abel is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Chemistry at the University of California, Berkeley and staff scientist in the Materials Science Division at LBL. He received a B. S. in Polymer Science and a Ph.D. in Polymer Science and Engineering (NSF Graduate Fellowship) from the University of Southern Mississippi. His Ph.D. work under the advisement of Prof. Charles McCormick focused on synthesizing stimuli-responsive water-soluble polymers using controlled radical polymerizations for applications such as drug delivery and oil/water remediation. Following his graduate studies, he worked as a postdoctoral researcher with Prof. Geoffrey Coates at Cornell University (2017-2021) where he developed bifunctional Lewis acid catalysts for the alternating ring-opening copolymerization of epoxides and cyclic anhydrides to synthesize well-defined polyesters. While at Cornell, he also developed new methods for living cationic ring-opening polymerization of cyclic acetals, enabling the synthesis of ultra-high molecular weight polyacetal thermoplastics with capable of near-quantitative chemical recycling back to monomer. His independent research interests lie in the areas of sustainable polymer organic chemistry, main group polymerization catalysis, and ionic ring-opening polymerizations.

events.title: Thesis Defense: Ben Charnay, Kanan Group
events.abstract:
"Understanding and Engineering Ion Transport: Molecular Mechanisms and Electrochemical Devices for Sustainability"
Ion transport governs the efficiency of electrochemical technologies central to a sustainable future, from electrolyzers to batteries and their recycling. In this talk, I will discuss how ion transport can be engineered at the device level and understood at the molecular level. I will first present a membrane-free cell, designed with the aid of ion transport modeling, that produces acid and base from water using a porous separator in place of ion exchange membranes. By exploiting competitive rather than selective transport, it tolerates impurities and requires less energy than membrane-based systems. I will show its application to CO₂ removal from air and to lithium-ion battery recycling, where it regenerates concentrated acid from Li₂SO₄ waste.
I will then examine how ions influence one another's transport in concentrated aqueous electrolytes. Using ultramicroelectrode measurements in tandem with ultrafast optical Kerr effect spectroscopy, I will show that alkali cations suppress hydroxide diffusion by up to 36% (K⁺ < Na⁺ < Li⁺), by slowing Grotthuss proton hopping.

events.title: Recent progress in Bridgeland stability conditions
events.abstract: Bridgeland stability conditions provide a powerful tool for studying complexes of coherent sheaves on algebraic varieties. I will discuss some recent progress on their existence, moduli spaces of stable objects, Bogomolov-type inequalities, and related applications.

events.title: How to construct a quantum Markov chain
events.abstract: Classical Markov chains and Monte Carlo methods have driven major advances in statistical physics, probability, and modern computation. In this talk, I will present a general construction of quantum Markov chains that provides both a rigorous quantum algorithmic framework for sampling Gibbs states and a physically consistent dynamical model of thermalization in noncommutative many-body quantum systems. Together, these perspectives reveal new mathematical challenges whose resolution could unlock useful early applications of quantum computers.

events.title: Cutoff V
Yuan Gao: TBA
Geometric configurations in sparse subsets of the integer lattice
events.abstract:
We study the problem of how dense a subset of the integer lattice can be without containing a similar copy of a given simplex. We give an overview of a functional analytic approach, that combines techniques of analytic number theory, the geometry of numbers and purely analytic tools, leading to power-saving bounds. Time permitting, we plan to discuss some extensions, such as configurations consisting of a simplex together with its barycentre - a geometric analogue of Roth’s theorem on three term arithmetic progressions.
This is joint work with Andrew Lott and Nagendar Reddy Ponagandla.

events.title: Support recovery of diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis
events.abstract: We study diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis with possibly large score estimation and discretization errors, and show that while they may not exactly recover the data distribution, they will recover the support (or data manifold). In continuous time, we show that even if the relative score estimation error is fixed (and not necessarily vanishing), then the rate at which the process approaches the support is $O(\sqrt{(T-t)|\log(T-t)|})$ as~$t \to T$, where~$T$ is the final time. In discrete time, we use geometric time steps with a fixed (non-vanishing) ratio and show that with a fixed relative score estimation error, the process approaches the data manifold exponentially with the number of iterations. The proof relies on controlling a Gaussian measure of a neighborhood of the cut-locus of the data manifold, which, in turn, uses arguments from computational real algebraic geometry. This is a joint work with A. Alieva, G. Iyer and A. Novikov.

events.title: Spectral graph methods in analytic number theory
events.abstract: The methods introduced in the breakthrough paper of Helfgott and Radziwill in 2021, and subsequently extended in my own work, have been instrumental in obtaining remarkable results in analytic number theory, including the recent resolution of the two-point Chowla conjecture. In this talk, I will give an introduction to these techniques.

Oscillation of graph eigenfunctions and its applications
events.abstract: Oscillation theory, originally due to Sturm, seeks to connect the number of sign changes of an eigenfunction of a self-adjoint operator to the label k of the corresponding eigenvalue. Its applications run in both directions: knowing k, one may wish to estimate the zero set, or the topology of its complement, useful in clustering and partitioning problems. Conversely, knowing an eigenvector (and thus the number of its sign changes), one may want to determine if it ist he ground state, useful in the linear stability analysis of solutions to nonlinear equations.Within the setting of generalized graph Laplacians, Fiedler's theorem says that the k-th eigenvector of a tree (a graph without cycles) changes sign across exactly k-1 edges. We present a formula for the number of sign changes on a general graph, which attributes the excess sign changes to the cycles in the graph and their intersections.This result has many interesting connections. First, it allows one to derive a simple formula for the effective mass tensor of a particular class of crystals (periodic lattices), namely the maximal abelian covers of finite graphs. Second, it can be used to efficiently determine stability of a stationary solution on a coupled oscillator network, such as the non-uniform Kuramoto model for the synchronization of a network of electrical oscillators. Finally, the determinant of the matrix which determines the excess sign changes is closely related to the graph's Kirchhoff polynomial (which counts the weighted spanning trees), hinting at connections to both Feynman amplitudes and matroids. Based on a joint work with Jared Bronski (UI Urbana-Champaign) and Mark Goresky (IAS Princeton).

events.title: An irreducible projective plane in 4-space
events.abstract: Until recently it was unknown whether every knotted projective plane in S^4 decomposes as a connected sum of a "trivial" projective plane and a knotted 2-sphere (the Kinoshita Conjecture). I'll talk about some classic constructions of knotted surfaces and how they motivated us to find an irreducible projective plane. This is joint work with Mark Hughes, Seungwon Kim, and Gheehyun Nahm.

events.title: Sharp time asymptotics in the nonlocal multi-dimensional Fisher-KPP equation
events.abstract: The problem under study is the evolution of the level sets in a nonlinear integro-differential equation, which involves a convolution kernel that is even, but not isotropic in space.One can show that the level sets expand in an asymptotically linear fashion, the asymptotic speed depending on the direction through an expression known as the Freidlin-Gärtner formula. The goal of the talk is to explore the corrections beyond the linear term.

events.title: Optimal Transport VI
A Mathematical Introduction to Inference
events.series: Student Learning Seminar on Mathematics and Computation
events.abstract: Inference is the computational process of running data through an AI model once it has been trained. It is a complex, dynamic problem which spans a deep technology stack. I will attempt to give a holistic view of inference, and then highlight some of its mathematical aspects.

events.title: Distinguishing statistics and shuffling cards
events.abstract: Distinguishing statistics are a fundamental tool for obtaining lower bounds on Markov chain mixing times. In this talk, we will give a general overview of the technique. Then we will provide some examples of its application to card shuffling. More specifically, we will discuss Uyemura-Reyes' work on the random-to-random shuffle in his Stanford PhD thesis, as well as my recent work on the shelf-shuffle and random-to-top shuffle. No prior knowledge of Markov chain mixing or card shuffling is assumed.

events.title: Stochastic Interacting Particle Methods and Generative Learning of Singularly Perturbed Advection-Reaction-Diffusion Equations
events.abstract: We first introduce a stochastic interacting particle (SIP) method for front speeds of Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov (KPP) equation based on variational principle and Feynman-Kac representation. Motivated by a genetic interpretation via particle resampling, we design a SIP algorithm for computing front spreading in general reactions and complex flows in 3D, with convergence analysis and examples. From the classical SIP (McKean-Vlasov process) for elliptic-parabolic Keller-Segel chemotaxis system, we develop a SIP-field algorithm to overcome memory issue (non-locality in time) in the fully parabolic setting and compute finite time blowup phenomenon efficiently. With simulated particle data over selected physical parameters, we train transport maps to predict solutions in the singular perturbation regime, by flow matching, optimal transport and their combination. Lastly, we show a scalable and efficient decomposition to approximate softmax attention in vision transformers based on asymptotic spreading and averaging in the long token limit.

events.title: Number Theory
The Theory of Probabilistically Checkable Proofs
events.abstract:
Speaker: Dor Minzer (MIT)
Abstract: I will discuss the theory of PCPs, from its inception in the early 1990's until the current state of affairs. Our discussion will be centered around the field of hardness of approximation, and in particular explain how the Unique-Games Conjecture arose and the human work that has been done towards proving it over the years. We will say a few words about OpenAI's recent resolution of the Unique-Games Conjecture.

events.title: Number Theory
Large deviations of Brownian intersections
events.abstract: In this talk, we consider the upper-tail large deviations of intersections of Brownian motions. Apart from intrinsic interest, these quantities are also closely related to the parabolic Anderson model via the Feynman-Kac formula. We prove that the occupation measures of Brownian motions conditioned to have large intersections converge weakly, up to spatial shifts, to the measure whose density is the square of an optimizer of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. The key tools are a compactification of the weak topology and an exponentially good approximation of the Brownian occupation measure.

events.title: Viehweg-Zuo I
Algebraic Geometry Seminar
Sturmian discrete and metric graphs - appearance and absence of gaps.
events.abstract: We study the spectra of Sturmian Schroedinger operators on graphs (either metric or discrete).A Sturmian sequence is an aperiodic sequence which is determined by an irrational frequency.These sequences are used to form aperiodic graph structures.We consider the integrated density of states (IDS) for Schroedinger operators on such graphs.The gap labelling theory predicts all the possible gaps in the spectra of these operators.We explicitly compute the gap labels; we show which gaps appear in the spectrum and which are absent, and why.The talk is based on joint works with Siegfried Beckus, Raphael Loewy and Gilad Sofer.

events.title: Capacities on dynamically convex toric domains and embedding obstructions
events.abstract: In this talk, I will introduce a sequence of symplectic capacities defined using cylindrical contact homology (CCH), based on unpublished work of Michael Hutchings and cobordism maps constructed by Hutchings and Jo Nelson. I will explain how topological constraints on holomorphic cylinders rule out certain terms in the CCH differential, while known capacity computations and cobordism maps force other terms to be nonzero. These arguments lead to explicit formulas for the differential and the capacities of four-dimensional monotone toric domains. I will conclude with examples of new symplectic embedding obstructions between monotone toric domains and discuss blind spots of CCH capacities.

events.title: Algebraic Geometry Seminar
The phase diagram of two-layer neural networks
events.abstract:
One of the most remarkable properties of modern AI systems is to learn and often memorize large training sets and yet generalize well to unseen data.
I will give an overview of work carried out over the past several years to undestand the interplay of overfitting and generalization in simple two layer networks.

events.title: Weak null singularity for the Einstein--Vlasov system
Bounded gaps between primes via APs with partly smooth moduli
events.abstract: Building on Yitang Zhang's work on bounded gaps between primes, the Polymath project showed that there are infinitely many prime gaps which are no larger than 246. In this talk I will discuss how the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem can be combined with newer equidistribution estimates for primes in APs to obtain an improvement on Polymath's result. The key ingredient is a new choice of support for the functions appearing in the corresponding optimization problem for the GPY sieve. To choose this support, we produce various equidistribution conditions for moduli with a large smooth factor, and reduce the calculation of relevant integrals to matrix multiplication and recursion.

events.title: Agentic AI for mathematical reasoning and verification
events.abstract: Well-designed agentic harnesses can substantially extend the capabilities of foundation models in mathematical reasoning and verification. I will illustrate this through case studies of three provers (Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos) and one verifier (OSVerify). I will also discuss the design philosophy behind these systems from a mathematician's perspective, and directions for future work.

Imagine a world where preparing food means implementing sophisticated recipes in an electric kitchen, and ingredients are approvisioned from a supermarket by car. In this world, when the car breaks down, or the supermarket is closed, or a power outage stops the appliances, or all recipes vanish, we'll believe we can't eat. events.title: Topology, Morse Index, and Area of Minimal Surfaces in Three-Manifolds
events.abstract: A foundational and fascinating theme in differential geometry is to understand how geometric quantities constrain topology. In this talk, we will explain how the topological complexity of minimal surfaces in closed three-manifolds can be controlled by their variational instability and area, and how positive Ricci or scalar curvature of the ambient manifold lead to stronger bounds depending only on the Morse index. Finally, we will discuss some consequences of these results for the topology of min–max minimal surfaces.

A quasipolynomial inverse theorem for the U^k(F_p^n) norm in the high characteristic
events.abstract: The inverse theory for Gowers uniformity norms is one of the central topics in additive combinatorics and one of the most important aspects of the theory is the question of bounds. In this talk, I will discuss a recent work, which proves a quasipolynomial inverse theorem for $mathsf{U}^k$ norm in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ in the case of high characteristic (meaning $p \geq k$). I will discuss the key ingredients of the argument: the abstract Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem, algebraic regularity method and the theory of multilinear maps defined on multilinear varieties. Along the way, I will highlight the differences from previous works in the inverse theory of uniformity norms.

Title: Charged Kaon Reconstruction in Neutrino-Argon Interactions in the NuMI Off-Axis Neutrino Beam at ICARUS
Abstract: The liquid argon (LAr) time projection chamber (TPC), or LArTPC, is an advanced neutrino detection technology, developed to detect and image neutrino interactions while assisting measurements of their fundamental properties. One such LArTPC, the ICARUS (Imaging Cosmic And Rare Underground Signals) detector at Fermilab, offers 480 tons of liquid argon as a target for neutrinos from two beams of neutrinos, the BNB (Booster Neutrino Beam) and off-axis NuMI (Neutrinos at the Main Injector) beam. These beams enable a variety of physics measurements, from neutrino oscillation to higher energy neutrino interactions. This thesis demonstrates the reconstruction of an understudied neutrino interaction product, the neutrino-induced charged kaon K+, using the tools provided by the SPINE reconstruction framework. Future measurements of atmospheric ν-induced K+ production, leveraging the techniques herein, would constrain a major background for proton decay at a number of experiments. While most neutrino interaction topologies are best identified by the particles closest to the interaction itself, K+ are best identified by their decays, often at rest, to µ+νµ. Inspired by this, we develop a novel particle flow proxy connecting all such potential decays to original interaction products. This yields a selection of K+ decay at rest to µ+νµ with a nominal Monte Carlo (MC) efficiency of 53% and purity of 84%. By leveraging this complete particle propagation information, we select 22 ν-induced K+ → µ+νµ candidates compared with nominal MC predictions of 11.0 signal and 2.17 background events. This represents the heretofore largest sample of selected K+ candidates in LAr [1]. These efficiencies, purities, and yields depend on the nominal simulation, which simulates all K+ production through strangeness preserving interactions and does not include single K+ production. Systematic uncertainties are not propagated, and no cross-section measurement or discovery significance is claimed. Additionally, as we will show, these ν-induced K+ and the other uncommon particles produced in such interactions present multiple unique detector calibration targets. Herein we demonstrate both the range distribution for the nominally monoenergetic decay µ+ as well as a dE/dx proxy for kaons, both new potential in-situ calibration sources for LArTPCs.

Advisor: Chao-Lin Kuo
