Title: Enabling Next-Generation Constraints on Cosmic Inflation via High Sensitivity Dust Measurements with BICEP Array and Lensing Template Construction with SPT-3G
Abstract: Measurements of B-mode polarization in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) sourced by primordial gravitational waves (PGWs) would constrain the energy scale and potential form of cosmic inflation. Two major obstacles to this measurement are polarized Galactic foregrounds, which produce B modes that can mimic a primordial signal, and gravitational lensing, which converts E modes into B modes. This dissertation presents work to mitigate both of these contaminants.Galactic foregrounds can be separated from the CMB via their different frequency spectra. The BICEP Array telescope observes with four small-aperture receivers, each observing at different frequency bands. We present the integration and performance of the 220/270 GHz receiver, designed to characterize Galactic dust, which was commissioned at Stanford from 2020 to 2024 and deployed to the South Pole in the 2024--2025 season.On the lensing side, we extend the curved-sky global minimum variance (GMV) lensing reconstruction pipeline with two foreground mitigation techniques, tSZ-deproj and cross-ILC, which target bias from the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich (tSZ) effect and the cosmic infrared background (CIB). Using SPT-3G simulations, these reduce the reconstruction bias at L < 1000 from ~ 4% to 2% and < 1%, respectively.We then develop foreground-robust lensing B-mode templates for delensing BICEP PGW results. Combining a profile-hardened GMV estimator with a Planck CIB tracer, we construct a lensing template whose foreground-induced bias is below 10% of the statistical uncertainty on its power spectrum. Simulations predict a residual delensed BB lensing power of ~ 48% of the original, over ell = [20, 200], corresponding to the highest delensing efficiency of any lensing template to date. These results will enable foreground-robust delensing in upcoming BICEP PGW analyses.

events.title: 2026 David O. Siegmund Lecture: Day 1
events.abstract:
The Lecture Committee for 2026 presents the next two installments of the David O. Siegmund Lecture Series. These special events are named for Professor Emeritus Siegmund to honor his accomplished career in methodological and applied statistical research, as well as his dedication as a mentor in his field.
Youssef Marzouk is the Breene M. Kerr (1951) Professor in Aeronautics and Astronautics at MIT, a core member of MIT's Statistics and Data Science Center, and a principal investigator in the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. He is also Associate Dean of the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. His research lies at the intersection of statistical inference, computational mathematics, and physical modeling. He develops new methodology for uncertainty quantification, Bayesian computation, and machine learning, motivated by applications across science and engineering. His recent work focuses on algorithms for inference, with applications to data assimilation and inverse problems; dimension reduction for high-dimensional learning and surrogate modeling; optimal experimental design; and measure transport as a tool for inference and generative modeling. He received his SB, SM, and PhD degrees from MIT and spent four years at Sandia National Laboratories before joining the MIT faculty in 2009.
Day 1: Understanding and learning conditioning operators for data assimilation
Data assimilation — encompassing a variety of sequential and possibly online inference tasks in state-space models — is a central challenge in geophysical modeling and other applications. Ensemble Kalman methods are remarkably successful workhorse algorithms in this setting. They approximate conditioning by transforming ensembles of prior samples into approximate posterior samples and are exact for jointly Gaussian distributions in the infinite-ensemble limit. This talk examines these algorithms through the lens of measure transport, seeking both to understand their effectiveness and to improve them.
First, we present new results on the bias of affine conditioning maps, with the stochastic ensemble Kalman update as a central example. We show that this update can be exact in the infinite-ensemble limit for a surprisingly broad class of non-Gaussian distributions. We then discuss systematic generalizations of the ensemble Kalman update and their approximation capabilities. Some of these generalizations use nonlinear triangular or block-triangular transport maps to enable conditioning by removing statistical dependence. These maps must be estimated from data, and interleaving map estimation and conditioning with dynamical evolution creates an interacting particle system. We identify the mean-field dynamics of such systems and establish quantitative, high-probability propagation-of-chaos bounds in Wasserstein distance.
Finally, we discuss ongoing work on learning conditioning operators that are amortized over both observations and input distributions. Our constructions use modern learning architectures to approximate measure-to-measure mappings, offering the prospect of flexible conditioning operators that can be reused across a range of data assimilation and Bayesian inverse problems.

events.title: Integrating statistics and AI for neuroscience research
events.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of the human brain, and their connections to neurological disorders, cognition, and normal development, is one of the most intriguing scientific questions. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and statistical methodology have created unprecedented opportunities, while many challenges remain. In this talk, I will provide an overview of several research directions pursued by our group integrating statistics and AI for neuroscience research. I will discuss how modern AI methods can facilitate statistical analysis of brain imaging data as well as how statistical principles can improve the development of AI models. I will illustrate with a number of case studies, highlighting the synergistic relationship between statistics and AI in advancing our understanding of the human brain.

events.title: Taming the statistical multiverse: Precise causal inference when reasonable analyses disagree
events.abstract:
When reasonable analyses of the same data conflict, it can be unclear what to conclude. We study one source of disagreement: which covariates to adjust for. Domain knowledge often leaves several adjustment sets plausible, and the resulting estimates can vary widely. Instead of asking how much conclusions vary for a fixed population, we ask: for which population do the covariate adjustments agree? We search for the closest such population, obtained by reweighting. For this population, we construct a single effect estimate and a confidence interval, valid if at least one candidate adjustment set satisfies ignorability. The interval's width shrinks at the usual 1/sqrt(n) rate, whereas disagreement among candidate analyses can persist even with arbitrarily large samples. In an application, our interval is about 77% narrower than the span of the candidate intervals. By changing the target population, we obtain precise inference even when it is unclear which covariates to adjust for.
This is based on joint work with Aditya Ghosh.

events.title: 2026 David O. Siegmund Lecture: Day 2
events.abstract:
The Lecture Committee for 2026 presents the next two installments of the David O. Siegmund Lecture Series. These special events are named for Professor Emeritus Siegmund to honor his accomplished career in methodological and applied statistical research, as well as his dedication as a mentor in his field.
Youssef Marzouk is the Breene M. Kerr (1951) Professor in Aeronautics and Astronautics at MIT, a core member of MIT's Statistics and Data Science Center, and a principal investigator in the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. He is also Associate Dean of the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. His research lies at the intersection of statistical inference, computational mathematics, and physical modeling. He develops new methodology for uncertainty quantification, Bayesian computation, and machine learning, motivated by applications across science and engineering. His recent work focuses on algorithms for inference, with applications to data assimilation and inverse problems; dimension reduction for high-dimensional learning and surrogate modeling; optimal experimental design; and measure transport as a tool for inference and generative modeling. He received his SB, SM, and PhD degrees from MIT and spent four years at Sandia National Laboratories before joining the MIT faculty in 2009.
Day 2: Designing dynamic measure transport for sampling and quantization
Sampling or otherwise summarizing complex probability distributions is a central task in statistics and machine learning. Many modern algorithms for this task introduce dynamics in the space of probability measures and design them to achieve good computational performance. We will discuss several aspects of this broad design endeavor, continuing the first day's theme of measure transport.
First, we consider the optimal scheduling of dynamic measure transport: at what speed should one proceed along a prescribed path of probability measures? Though many popular methods seek trajectories with zero acceleration in a Lagrangian frame, we show how specific "curved" trajectories can improve approximation and learning. We then present extensions of this idea that seek not only schedules but paths that improve the spatial regularity of the underlying velocity field.
Second, we discuss weighted quantization, i.e., summarizing a complex distribution with a small set of weighted points. We study this problem by minimizing maximum mean discrepancy via gradient flow in the Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao geometry. Rather than discretizing the flow, we use its equilibrium conditions to derive a fixed-point algorithm called mean shift interacting particles (MSIP). We show that MSIP outperforms state-of-the-art methods for quantizing empirical distributions and, moreover, enables the construction of weighted quantizations given only an unnormalized density.

events.title: Generative AI and the Future of FPGA IP Development
events.abstract:
Abstract/Description:
The development of intellectual property (IP) for field-programmable gate arrays has traditionally relied on lengthy, manual cycles of specification, RTL design, verification, and timing closure. Generative AI is now altering each of these stages. This talk focuses on three areas in which the presenter has observed dramatic change in workflow: design space exploration, RTL generation, and timing signoff.
The presentation will outline the methodology adopted at Lattice Semiconductor and will review several success stories in which generative AI shortened development schedules and improved engineering productivity. Particular attention will be given to the practical aspects of the approach: where AI-assisted design delivers measurable value, where human architectural judgment remains essential, and how correctness and quality are assured in a hardware context where errors are costly.
Although the talk will not address testbench and verification creation or documentation in detail, similar implications apply in those domains, and many of the lessons presented will carry over to them. The broader implications for engineering education and research, including the skills future hardware engineers will require and the open problems that merit academic investigation, will be reserved for the question-and-answer session, where the speaker welcomes a candid, open discussion with the audience.
Speaker/Bio:
Rick Crotty is Senior Fellow and Chief FPGA Architect at Lattice Semiconductor, a position he has held since 2019. In this role, he guides the architectural direction of Lattice’s FPGA product portfolio.
From 2014 to 2019, he co-founded Andapt, Inc., an analog mixed-signal power management IC (PMIC) company. There he pioneered the use of FPGA-based control loops within PMIC silicon, bringing together programmable logic and power management.
Prior to Andapt, he spent 21 years at Xilinx, Inc., where he held a series of roles in FPGA applications, circuit design, and ultimately FPGA architecture. Across more than three decades in the industry, his career has spanned the full range of programmable logic, from circuit-level implementation to system-level architecture. He is a named inventor on 45 patents in FPGA and circuit design technologies.
He holds a B.S. in Electrical Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University and an M.S. in Computer Engineering from Santa Clara University.
